finding.claim: Authorization bypass on DELETE /files/<fid>. views.py imports the boolean `is_allowed` under the alias `require_allowed` and calls it without using the result or aborting. The check never blocks anything, so any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Any request to DELETE /files/<fid>, including an unauthenticated one with no X-Session-User-Verified header (g.user = None), and any fid that exists in STORE.

trace.note: `is_allowed` is imported as `require_allowed`, which hides that it returns a bool and does not abort
delete_file(fid) loads the file from STORE with no ownership check
`require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete")` returns False for unauthorized users and the return value is discarded
`is_allowed` only returns a bool; `ensure_allowed` (acl.py:8) is the version that calls abort(403)

finding.guards_checked: Sibling rename_file (views.py:26) correctly uses `ensure_allowed`, which aborts with 403, so the delete route is the outlier. No other auth middleware exists; before_request only sets g.user (views.py:10-12). The return value of the check is unused and there is no abort.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: is_allowed (aliased require_allowed) returns a bool that is discarded; before_request only sets g.user; no other middleware
verdict.reason: views.py:18 calls the bool-returning `is_allowed` (imported as `require_allowed` at views.py:4, defined at acl.py:4) as a bare statement, so `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19 runs for any caller, including anonymous ones, unlike `ensure_allowed` (acl.py:8-10, used at views.py:26), which aborts with 403.

finding.claim: User identity is taken straight from the client-supplied request header `X-Session-User-Verified`. Nothing in the repo verifies a session, signature or token, or strips the header. If the app is reachable without a trusted proxy that sets and overwrites this header, any client can impersonate any user named in a resource's grants. That includes the rename route, whose ACL check is otherwise enforced.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, controlled by the client.
finding.sink: `ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` at views.py:26, followed by the rename at views.py:27. The ACL lookup at acl.py:5 trusts the spoofed name.

trace.note: g.user is set from the raw header with no verification
ensure_allowed uses g.user as the identity
The grants lookup is keyed on the attacker-chosen user string

finding.guards_checked: I found no signature, session or token validation and no header stripping in the two files in this repo. A fronting proxy that sets and overwrites the header might exist, but it is not visible here. Because I could not confirm it, this is conditional on that deployment assumption.

verdict.guard_found: none in repo. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 correctly, but it only checks the spoofable g.user. The delete route's require_allowed is an alias of the bool-returning is_allowed with its result discarded (views.py:18), which is a separate bug.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user from the raw client header with no verification, and acl.py:5 looks up grants by that string, so any client who knows a granted username passes ensure_allowed at views.py:26 and reaches the rename at views.py:27. This holds unless an external proxy overwrites the header, and that proxy is not in the repo.
